title: PayPal Built Its Moat on a Checkout Button That AI Agents Will Never Click
subtitle: The profit engine of online commerce is fading while management promises replacement revenue by 2028
summary: Artificial intelligence agents assembling shopping carts threaten to bypass the familiar branded checkout button that generates most of PayPal's high-margin earnings. While the company joins every emerging AI commerce directory, its core growth engine continues to decelerate years before new revenue streams can arrive.

bodyHtml:
PayPal runs the familiar orange button resting at the bottom of digital checkout pages. When you buy concert tickets or renew your gym membership online, you click that button and skip typing sixteen credit card digits. PayPal takes a lucrative toll on the transaction. It is an empire constructed on conditioned reflex: roughly 440 million consumer accounts trained over a quarter-century to trust one specific click.

Behind that click sit two very different engines. Branded checkout is the pristine tollbooth, generating high-margin profit dollars from people instinctively tapping the logo. Braintree is the unglamorous plumbing beneath other corporate storefronts, processing cards invisibly at much lower margins. Venmo handles social payments, and financial services sells credit and debit cards. PayPal is essentially a luxury landlord whose prime retail strip generates all the real profit, while its discount warehouse in the back does most of the heavy lifting.

That prime strip is facing an existential tenant problem because artificial intelligence is changing how carts get filled. In agentic commerce, an AI assistant shops across the web, negotiates terms, and completes payment autonomously. No human eyeballs scan the screen, no thumb hovers over an orange icon, and nobody cares about brand nostalgia. When an algorithm pays, your decades of muscle memory become obsolete code.

PayPal understands this threat and has methodically signed every agentic partnership going. It launched with OpenAI, joined Microsoft's Copilot Checkout as one of three trusted rails, plugged into Google's Universal Commerce Protocol, and joined Meta's Muse assistant. Its developer suite, Agent Ready, connects smoothly across competing models. But being an available option on a pull-down menu inside ChatGPT is not the same as owning the entire checkout screen. Stripe and Shopify are already the default plumbing on those platforms, leaving PayPal as just another row in an API directory.

That commoditization arrived right after PayPal lost its most credible exit ramp. In July, a consortium led by Stripe and private-equity firm Advent made a formal takeover offer at $60.50 per share in cash, valuing PayPal at $53.4 billion. PayPal's board resisted, holding out for a better valuation. By late August, the bidders walked away and the stock tumbled roughly 13% in a single session. PayPal was left alone to face the very firm that had just tried to buy it, which also happens to co-author the Agentic Commerce Protocol.

Meanwhile, the numbers confirm that the traditional button is sputtering. Branded checkout payment volume grew just 1% currency-neutral in the third quarter, holding between 1% and 2% for four consecutive quarters. Chief Executive Enrique Lores acknowledged the structural shift to investors, noting that "this algorithm does not require it to return fully to historical growth rates." Translated plainly: the button isn't coming back.

The problem for equity holders is the bridge between that decaying core and whatever comes next. On his summer call, Lores offered a sobering timeline. Agentic payments and digital identity, he said, become "increasingly meaningful contributors to our business" only looking to 2028 and beyond. A tech stock cannot easily defend its valuation when its historic cash machine is cooling off today and the replacement revenue is penciled in for 2028.

The short thesis is ruthless because it attacks the quality of PayPal's underlying numbers. Non-GAAP net income actually slipped 3% last quarter to $1.25 billion, yet earnings per share jumped 8% solely because management spent billions retiring over 10% of the company's share count. Total revenue grew at just 2% while volume climbed 6%, a stark mechanical indicator that low-margin processing volume is cannibalizing high-margin branded transactions. When you strip out Venmo, Barclays estimates branded checkout volume was completely flat. With European regulators at Germany's Federal Cartel Office formally challenging PayPal's merchant anti-surcharging rules this month, the company's pricing umbrella is eroding right as agentic traffic takes off.

Bulls will counter that the market has already written PayPal off as roadkill, pricing the equity at barely 10 times forward earnings with a free cash flow yield near 13%. Venmo's debit card usage is up more than 50%, and financial services now drives over a fifth of transaction margin dollars. Furthermore, Lores makes a fair point about structural inertia: "When PayPal started, the key value proposition was around trust and security. This was needed in e-commerce. This will be even more needed in agentic commerce." Autonomous software agents will inevitably encounter disputed charges, identity theft, and fraudulent storefronts, leaving deep-pocketed balance sheets with dedicated dispute resolution as essential intermediaries.

To re-rate, the stock must prove that branded checkout can sustain low-single-digit growth without relying on financial engineering, while showing that consumer adoption of automated agents remains fragmented. We will see whether that thesis holds in the fourth-quarter release, where any branded checkout print below 1% would confirm that the core engine is rolling over.

Being present on every list is cold comfort when software agents choose their own favorites.
